agentCan: Build the authorization-code flow and token-info validation
Key stored tokens by user and blog, and handle silent revocation (tokens dying when users revoke)

approval.cost: None stated in the documentation read
approval.trigger: No vendor review or approval step could be verified from the official documentation read. Nothing in the Automattic documentation read (the Gravatar developer docs describing this same OAuth2 system end-to-end, and the official Make WordPress mobile handbook) mentions any approval, review, cap, fee, or marketplace/listing step between registering the Application and having arbitrary users authorize it; the documented flow goes straight from app registration to user authorization. Who approves access: the end user, at the authorize step (per-user consent). No admin-consent concept is documented. Caveat: the portal's own OAuth2 guide page could not be read in this pass (see Evidence), so treat 'no review required' as highly likely but not fully verified.
approval.wait: None documented (no review step to attach a timeline to)

blockers.detail: Because code-grant tokens do not expire and no refresh token is issued, a leaked token stays valid until the user revokes the app's access from their WordPress.com account settings. Your integration must handle tokens dying unexpectedly when users revoke.
blockers.howToClear: Use the token-info endpoint to validate tokens, and design re-authorization recovery for revoked tokens.
blockers.title: No refresh token: revocation is the only off-ramp

blockers.detail: The token response carries a specific blog_id and blog_url: a token obtained through the standard flow is bound to one site, not to everything the user owns. A SaaS connecting many users must key stored tokens by user AND blog (multi-site users produce multiple authorizations).
blockers.howToClear: Store blog_id/blog_url with every token and treat each blog as its own connection.
blockers.title: Blog-scoped tokens by default

blockers.detail: Exchanging the code from the browser both fails (CORS) and leaks the client_secret; the token POST is strictly server-side for web apps. The password grant cannot help: it is owner-only testing ('this is only available to you as the application owner and not to any other user... meant for testing purposes only'), and an app owner using two-step authentication must use an application password with it.
blockers.howToClear: Keep the secret and the exchange on your server, always.
blockers.title: Secret-handling trap

Automattic frames it as the weaker option: 'This is an alternative to Server Authentication but not as safe, so consider using Server Authentication instead.' Tokens currently last two weeks)

Password grant (grant_type=password): documented ONLY for the application owner, for testing: 'this is only available to you as the application owner and not to any other user. This is meant for testing purposes only'
flavor.recommended: The server-side Authorization Code flow on a WordPress.com Application
flavor.why: The object is an Application registered in the WordPress.com developer portal at developer.wordpress.com/apps/ (log in with a WordPress.com account, 'Create New Application'; issued a Client ID and Client Secret). One developer-owned Application serves all end users; each user authorizes that same Application against their own WordPress.com account. The OAuth 2.0 endpoints live on the API domain: authorize at public-api.wordpress.com/oauth2/authorize, token at public-api.wordpress.com/oauth2/token, validation at public-api.wordpress.com/oauth2/token-info. Automattic's guidance (in its Gravatar developer docs, which run on this same WordPress.com OAuth2 system): 'Code should be used for server-side applications where you can guarantee that secrets will be stored securely.' It is also the only flavor whose tokens don't expire.

humanMust: Create a WordPress.com account (if you don't already have one)

Register the Application at developer.wordpress.com/apps/ (name, description, website URL, Redirect URLs; 'We don't force you to fill in all the fields, but you will need all of them to get your access token properly')
name: WordPress.com
nuances: Implicit-flow trap: implicit tokens 'currently last two weeks, and users will need to authenticate with your app once they expire'; 'Use the expires_in fragment to detect when you should prompt for a refresh', where 'refresh' means re-running the authorization, not a refresh-token grant.

Redirect URI exactness: the redirect_uri must match one registered in the application settings, and at token exchange it 'must match the redirect_uri used during the Authorize step'; a mismatch fails the exchange. If the user denies authorization, the redirect includes an access_denied parameter.

Token validation: GET public-api.wordpress.com/oauth2/token-info?client_id=...&token=... returns the client_id, user_id, blog_id, and scope for a valid token and errors if the token wasn't authorized for your application.
Scopes are passed as indexed arrays in the authorize URL (scope[0]=...&scope[1]=...), an unusual encoding detail that breaks naive OAuth libraries.
prerequisites: A WordPress.com account for the developer portal
Application settings completed (name, description, website URL, Redirect URLs)
A server-side token store keyed by user and blog

steps.detail: Log in with a WordPress.com account and choose 'Create New Application'; fill in the application settings (name, description, website URL, Redirect URLs). The registration yields the Client ID and Client Secret.
steps.title: Register the Application

steps.detail: Send the user to public-api.wordpress.com/oauth2/authorize with URL-encoded client_id, redirect_uri (must match one defined in the application settings), response_type=code, and scope (multiple scopes as indexed arrays, e.g. scope[0]=...&scope[1]=...). The user logs in and approves or denies (denial returns an access_denied parameter).
steps.title: Send the user to the authorize endpoint

steps.detail: Server-side POST to public-api.wordpress.com/oauth2/token with client_id, client_secret, redirect_uri (must match the Authorize-step value), code, and grant_type=authorization_code. The JSON response is { access_token, blog_id, blog_url, token_type: 'bearer' }, bound to a specific blog, with NO refresh token (code-grant tokens do not expire).
steps.title: Exchange the code server-side

steps.detail: Call the WordPress.com REST API at public-api.wordpress.com/rest/v1.1/... with Authorization: Bearer. Optionally validate tokens via the token-info endpoint.
steps.title: Call the API with the Bearer token

tagline: A real OAuth 2.0 program with an unusual token model: authorization-code tokens never expire and no refresh token is issued, tokens are scoped to a single blog by default, and no vendor review is documented (the portal's own docs could not be read in this pass, see Evidence).

time.active: ~10 min of app registration + ~1 hr of flow code
time.total: Same day; no approval wait documented
